analysis.one_liner: Lets consumers deduct lawyer fees from winnings in consumer protection lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee from June 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When a consumer wins a lawsuit against a debt collector, a predatory lender, or a company that broke consumer protection laws, part of the award goes to their attorney. Under current tax law that fee is taxed as if the consumer kept it, because the only way to deduct it was eliminated by the 2017 tax law. This bill creates a straightforward deduction, taken before income is calculated, so consumers are not taxed on money they never received. It covers claims under major consumer laws including the Truth in Lending Act, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who win judgments or settlements for consumer protection violations. They would no longer pay income tax on attorney fees and court costs deducted from their winnings, keeping more of what they were awarded.

how_it_helps.text: Allows an above-the-line deduction for attorney fees and court costs connected to a consumer protection claim, so the fees are not taxed as income to the consumer [S2][S3].

Covers a broad set of consumer laws, including the Truth in Lending Act, Fair Credit Reporting Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and protections for servicemembers, plus any federal, state, or local law regulating consumer transactions [S3].
Applies to fees and costs paid in years after enactment, for judgments or settlements in those years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that lose consumer protection lawsuits would face somewhat more and stronger claims, since consumers who keep more of an award are more willing to sue. The federal government would collect somewhat less tax from winning consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collectors, lenders, and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The deduction reduces federal tax revenue, and the bill was introduced without an estimate or offset of that cost [S1][S2].

The coverage is very broad — it sweeps in any state or local consumer transaction claim — so the deduction could apply to large settlements in high-fee cases, and the fiscal cost depends on how widely it is used [S3].

A simpler alternative would be to exclude attorney fees from taxable income outright; a deduction still only helps people who owe tax at their own rate and requires them to itemize the calculation correctly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix is sound and narrow in intent: people should not pay tax on money that went straight to their lawyer. The main tradeoff is unquantified federal revenue loss and an unusually broad definition of covered claims that could reach large settlements. The bill's real weakness was not its design but its neglect — it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Horsford introduced the bill in the House on June 11, 2020 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].
The bill had one cosponsor, Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia [S4][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that lose consumer protection lawsuits — debt collectors, consumer lenders, and credit reporting agencies — avoided the added litigation exposure this bill would have created, and winning consumers kept paying tax on attorney fees deducted from their awards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors, lenders, and credit bureaus

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill after its June 2020 referral, so it never received a floor vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill's only two sponsors were House Democrats, so no cross-party or floor-vote pattern exists in the record.

industries.industry: Debt collectors, consumer lenders, and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: These companies are the most common defendants in consumer protection suits, and lawsuits are a main way consumers recover for wrongful collections, credit report errors, and abusive lending. Making it cheaper for consumers to sue — by letting them deduct attorney fees — increases their exposure, which is why their interest here runs against the bill's benefit to consumers.

industries.industry: Consumer-side attorneys and legal aid practices
industries.note: Attorneys working consumer cases would see their fees deducted pre-tax, and clients who keep more of an award are more able and willing to bring meritorious claims. Their gain tracks directly with the consumer's gain.
